literature_reinforcement.project: A Music Box to Help Babies Sleep — intrauterine bed (blood-flow noise layer) literature reinforcement
literature_reinforcement.scope: Primary measured literature on intrauterine acoustics: (a) in-utero SPL by frequency band, (b) external-to-uterus transfer / frequency-dependent attenuation, (c) intrauterine background-noise spectra. Numbers are extracted only from primary abstracts or full texts (PubMed / PMC / journal pages). Secondary-review summary numbers were NOT adopted. Derived values (my own arithmetic from extracted endpoints) are kept in a separate derived_values section and are not presented as extracted data.

paper.authors: Gerhardt KJ, Abrams RM, Oliver CC
paper.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
paper.title: Sound environment of the fetal sheep
paper.subjects_and_method: Pregnant ewes; hydrophone surgically implanted inside the intact amnion. Sound pressure levels measured outside and inside the ewe during quiet and during sound-field exposures to broadband and octave-band noise; attenuation through maternal tissues and fluids calculated.

measurement.quantity: variation of sound pressure with position inside the amnion (maximum)
internal noise floor, no external sound (minimum)

paper.quote: Sound pressures generated by low frequencies (less than 0.25 kHz) were 2 to 5 dB greater inside than outside the ewe. Above 0.25 kHz, sound attenuation increased at a rate of 6 dB per octave. For 4.0 kHz, sound attenuation averaged 20 dB. The sound pressure recorded at different locations within the amnion with respect to the sound source varied by up to 6 dB. The internal noise floor in the absence of externally generated sounds was as low as 50 dB (spectrum level) above 0.2 kHz.
paper.slope_evaluation: The only primary abstract in this search that states a transfer slope directly: 6 dB per octave above 250 Hz (sheep). Caveat: animal model, and the statement is an average trend, not band-by-band data.

paper.authors: Richards DS, Frentzen B, Gerhardt KJ, McCann ME, Abrams RM
paper.title: Sound levels in the human uterus
paper.doi: not shown on the PubMed record
paper.subjects_and_method: 8 parturients (women in labor); hydrophone placed in the uterus. Sound pressure levels measured for externally generated one-third-octave band noises, male and female voices, and the subject's own voice.
paper.quote: Low-frequency sounds (0.125 kHz) generated outside the mother were enhanced by an average of 3.7 dB. There was a gradual increase in attenuation for increasing frequencies, with a maximum attenuation of 10.0 dB at 4.0 kHz. Intrauterine sound levels of the mother's voice were enhanced by an average of 5.2 dB, whereas external male and female voices were attenuated by 2.1 and 3.2 dB, respectively.
paper.slope_evaluation: Human in-vivo band endpoints (enhancement at 125 Hz, maximum attenuation at 4 kHz). The abstract gives endpoints only; intermediate one-third-octave bands are in the full text, not the abstract. An endpoint-to-endpoint average slope computed from these endpoints is recorded under derived_values, not as extracted data.

paper.authors: Benzaquen S, Gagnon R, Hunse C, Foreman J
paper.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
paper.title: The intrauterine sound environment of the human fetus during labor
paper.subjects_and_method: 10 pregnant women near term in labor; intrauterine background noise measured with a miniaturized hydrophone placed transcervically at the level of the fetal neck under ultrasonographic guidance. Values below are for the 8 women in whom no cardiovascular noise was audible.
paper.quote: the intrauterine noise consisted predominantly of low-frequency noise (less than 100 Hz) from 60 to 85 dB. Above 100 Hz, the sound pressure level was less than 60 dB, decreasing to 40 dB above 500 Hz.
paper.slope_evaluation: This is the spectrum of the intrauterine background noise itself (human), not a transfer function. It grounds the bed layer's own spectral shape (the bed imitates the background), but it must not be cited as the external-to-uterus transfer slope. Values above 100 Hz are stated as inequalities (bounds), so any slope computed from them is approximate; see derived_values.

paper.authors: Gélat P, David AL, Haqshenas SR, Henriques J, Thibaut de Maisières A, White T, Jauniaux E
paper.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
paper.title: Evaluation of fetal exposure to external loud noise using a sheep model: quantification of in utero acoustic transmission across the human audio range
paper.subjects_and_method: 6 time-mated pregnant Romney ewes (103-130 days gestation), in vivo; calibrated hydrophone sutured to the fetal occiput inside the amniotic sac; external white-noise source; acoustic transfer functions measured from 100 Hz to 20 kHz in 6 Hz steps (finest frequency resolution in this literature). Reference microphones in the operating theatre; the authors note theatre reverberation (room modes) as a limitation.

measurement.quantity: sound pressure level inside the amniotic sac, broadband white noise (ewe 2)
broadband level difference, inside amniotic sac vs operating-theatre microphones (ewe 2)

paper.quote: Measurement of acoustic transmission through the maternal abdominal and uterine walls indicates that frequency contents above 10 kHz are transmitted into the amniotic sac, and that some frequencies are attenuated by as little as 3 dB.

In 1 ewe, a hydrophone inserted inside the amniotic sac recorded a 4 dB attenuation between 200 Hz and 400 Hz, with respect to a microphone inside the operating theater, placed near the body of the ewe.

The results of the present study indicate that at specific frequencies, the abdominal wall together with overlying tissue and the amniotic fluid provide as little as 2–3 dB acoustic attenuation of external airborne sound inside the uterine environment at frequencies below 1 kHz, confirming the results of previous studies. Above 1 kHz, the attenuation increases to 20–40 dB, depending on the animal and position of the external microphone. Above 10 kHz, the improved measurement protocol used in this study reveals that significant external sound is transmitted in utero and that attenuation is as little 3 dB at 11 kHz in one ewe.
the sound pressure level inside the amniotic sac is therefore 101 dB (ie, only 5–6 dB lower than at the 2 operating theater microphone locations)
paper.slope_evaluation: Usable, and it contradicts any single straight-line slope: the measured transfer is nearly flat below 1 kHz (as little as 2-3 dB), drops to 20-40 dB above 1 kHz, and recovers above 8-10 kHz (internal resonances; only 3 dB at 11 kHz in one ewe). A single dB/octave slope is therefore an idealization of this curve, not the curve itself. Caveats stated by the authors: inter-animal variability and operating-theatre reverberation in the reference microphones.

paper.authors: Gélat P, van't Wout E, Haqshenas R, Melbourne A, David AL, Mufti N, Henriques J, Thibaut de Maisières A, Jauniaux E
paper.title: Evaluation of fetal exposure to environmental noise using a computer-generated model
paper.subjects_and_method: Computational (boundary-element) model built from MRI anatomy of 4 pregnant patients (from 24 weeks of gestation); NOT a measurement. Included because it is the only model found in scope and it quantifies the same transfer; its numbers depend on assumed tissue attenuation coefficients.

measurement.quantity: transmitted sound pressure level relative to incident wave at uterus barycentre (Subjects 2 and 3)
transmitted sound pressure level relative to incident wave at uterus barycentre (Subject 4)
transmitted sound pressure level relative to incident wave at uterus barycentre (Subject 1)
transmission deviation from incident wave, high-attenuation-coefficient case, uterus barycentre (Subjects 2 and 3)

paper.quote: Our calculations show that the sound transmitted in utero is attenuated by as little as 6 dB below 1 kHz, confirming results from animal studies that the maternal abdomen and pelvis do not shelter the fetus from external noise.

At the midrange frequency of 1 kHz, we note that the transmitted sound pressure level is 9 dB above that of the incident wave for datasets associated with Subjects 2 and 3, 7 dB above for Subject 4, and 6 dB for Subject 1.

For the calculations employing the higher attenuation coefficient in the uterus in Fig. 2A, D, G, J, the resonances are dampened, as expected, but the transmission remains within 15 dB of the incident wave across the human audio range in datasets associated with Subjects 2 and 3 when considering the acoustic pressure magnitude sampled at the uterus barycentre.
paper.slope_evaluation: Model output, not a measurement: it cannot serve as measured grounding for a slope. It is consistent with the in-vivo finding that the transfer below 1 kHz is much flatter than the classic slope, and it even predicts enhancement (+6 to +9 dB) at 1 kHz from internal reflections.

paper.authors: Peters AJM, Abrams RM, Gerhardt KJ, Griffiths SK
paper.journal: Journal of Low Frequency Noise, Vibration and Active Control
paper.title: Transmission of airborne sound from 50-20,000 Hz into the abdomen of sheep
paper.subjects_and_method: 5 sheep; airborne sound from 50 to 20,000 Hz at stimulus levels of 90 to 110 dB SPL; attenuation into the abdomen measured as a function of frequency and stimulus level.
paper.quote: Sound attenuation varied as a function of frequency (p<0.001). Additionally, in the 800-2,000 Hz range there was enhancement of sound pressure of up to 10 dB.
paper.slope_evaluation: The abstract reports no band-by-band attenuation values, so no slope can be derived from it. Its mid-band enhancement (800-2,000 Hz) is independent evidence that the transfer is non-monotonic, i.e. not a single straight slope.

paper.authors: Querleu D, Renard X, Versyp F, Paris-Delrue L, Crépin G
paper.journal: European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology
paper.title: Fetal hearing
paper.subjects_and_method: Review article (PubMed publication type: Review) summarizing the group's human intrauterine recordings and the wider literature.

measurement.quantity: attenuation of external sounds (general upper bound)

paper.quote: Animal experiments as well as investigations in the human lead to the conclusion that sounds from outside the mother are attenuated, but rarely by more than 30 decibels; external conversations are audible.
paper.slope_evaluation: No band values in the primary abstract, so no slope grounding. NOTE (unverified lead, deliberately NOT extracted as data): secondary literature (e.g. Muenssinger et al. 2013, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, PMC3876038) attributes band values of 2 dB at 250 Hz, 14 dB at 500 Hz, 20 dB at 1000 Hz and 26 dB at 2000 Hz to this group's hydrophone measurements. These could not be confirmed in a primary source within this search (the underlying primary reports are in French journals: Querleu et al. 1981, J Gynécol Obstét Biol Reprod 10:307-314; Querleu et al. 1988, Rev Fr Gynécol Obstét 83:43-50) and are therefore recorded only as a lead, not as extracted values.

paper.authors: Smith CV, Satt B, Phelan JP, Paul RH
paper.title: Intrauterine sound levels: intrapartum assessment with an intrauterine microphone
paper.subjects_and_method: 9 term gravid volunteers after amniorrhexis (membrane rupture); electrically isolated microphone placed in the uterus (not a hydrophone in intact fluid). Baseline levels and response to transabdominal vibroacoustic stimulation with an artificial larynx.

measurement.quantity: peak mixed-frequency sound level during vibroacoustic stimulation (artificial larynx)

paper.quote: Baseline levels of intrauterine sound were 72 to 88 db. Transabdominal vibroacoustic stimulation with an artificial larynx produced peak mixed frequency sound levels of 91 to 111 db.
paper.slope_evaluation: Broadband levels only; no frequency-band values. Useful only as an overall background-level reference.

paper.authors: Gerhardt KJ, Abrams RM, Kovaz BM, Gomez KJ, Conlon M
paper.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
paper.title: Intrauterine noise levels produced in pregnant ewes by sound applied to the abdomen
paper.subjects_and_method: Pregnant ewes; an electronic artificial larynx or a standard audiometric earphone applied directly to the abdominal surface (contact source); sound transmission assessed with a hydrophone near the ear of the fetus within the intact amnion.

measurement.quantity: sound pressure at hydrophone, electronic artificial larynx directly over hydrophone (average)
sound pressure at hydrophone, audiometric earphone (highest)

paper.quote: Sound pressures produced by the electronic artificial larynx located directly over the hydrophone averaged 134.9 dB, whereas the highest sound pressure produced by a similarly placed earphone was 95.2 dB.
paper.slope_evaluation: Contact-source levels at one position, with a strong distance effect; no frequency-band attenuation. Not usable for the airborne transfer slope.

paper.authors: Armitage SE, Baldwin BA, Vince MA
paper.title: The fetal sound environment of sheep
paper.subjects_and_method: Hydrophones implanted inside the intact amniotic sac of 2 pregnant ewes; sounds available to fetal lambs recorded.
paper.no_numbers_reason: The PubMed abstract contains no numeric values (it reports qualitatively that external conversation-level sounds were picked up without masking by maternal cardiovascular sounds). Band values: none confirmed. A secondary review (Verny 1989) reports an average attenuation of 20 dB with a maximum of 37 dB at 1000 Hz for this study, but this was not verified in the primary source and was not adopted.
paper.quote: Hydrophones implanted inside the intact amniotic sac recorded sounds available to fetal lambs.
paper.slope_evaluation: No numbers in the primary abstract; the 2-page report's figure data were not accessible in this search.

paper.authors: Vince MA, Billing AE, Baldwin BA, Toner JN, Weller C
paper.title: Maternal vocalizations and other sounds in the fetal lamb's sound environment
paper.subjects_and_method: Miniature radio hydrophone implanted in the amniotic sac of 3 ewes; recordings from 3 weeks before birth through delivery.
paper.no_numbers_reason: The abstract (as reproduced in the APA PsycNET record of the journal abstract) contains no numeric band values; it reports qualitatively that the mother's voice was slightly louder at the intra-amniotic hydrophone than at a microphone beside her flank.

quote.source: Journal abstract via APA PsycNET record

paper.quote: Results indicate that the sound of the mother's voice was slightly louder when picked up by the hydrophone inside the amniotic sac than when picked up by a microphone beside her flank.
paper.slope_evaluation: No numbers; qualitative support only for low-frequency/voice enhancement.

paper.authors: Walker D, Grimwade J, Wood C
paper.journal: American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology
paper.title: Intrauterine noise: a component of the fetal environment
paper.subjects_and_method: 16 pregnant women; condenser microphone (not a hydrophone) placed in the cervical canal / lateral to the fetal head, before and after membrane rupture.
paper.no_numbers_reason: No PubMed abstract text is available for this record, and band values could not be confirmed from the primary text within this search. A US National Academies report (secondary) discusses this study's transmission-loss figure but flags methodological caveats (microphone correction; possible gas-bubble resonance around 500 Hz); those secondary values were not adopted.
paper.slope_evaluation: Unverified in the primary source within this search.

paper.authors: Nyman M, Arulkumaran S, Hsu TS, Ratnam SS, Till O, Westgren M
paper.title: Vibroacoustic stimulation and intrauterine sound pressure levels
paper.subjects_and_method: Human intrauterine sound pressure measurement during vibroacoustic stimulation (bibliographic details confirmed from multiple citing reference lists).
paper.no_numbers_reason: The primary abstract could not be retrieved within this search, so no values were extracted. Recorded as an unresolved item rather than filled from secondary citations.

derived_values.note: My own arithmetic from extracted endpoints. These are NOT extracted data and are excluded from the verbatim-quote check; they are included so the slope discussion in the memo is transparent.

derived.description: Endpoint-to-endpoint average transfer slope between 125 Hz (+3.7 dB enhancement, i.e. -3.7 dB attenuation) and 4000 Hz (10.0 dB attenuation): total change 13.7 dB over log2(4000/125) = 5 octaves, giving approximately 2.7 dB per octave. This assumes a straight line between the two endpoints, which the paper itself does not claim.

Rough estimate of the background spectrum's fall between 100 Hz (upper bound 60 dB) and 500 Hz (40 dB): 20 dB over log2(500/100) = 2.32 octaves, giving approximately 8.6 dB per octave. Because the 100 Hz figure is an upper bound (less than 60 dB), this is an approximate lower-bound-style estimate of steepness, not a measured slope. This describes the background noise itself, not a transfer function.

verification.check_a_quote_containment: Method: a Python script parsed this XML and, for every numeric token in every measurement (value / value_min / value_max), searched for that token with digit/dot boundaries in the same paper's stored verbatim quote text. Result: 38 of 38 numeric tokens found in their own paper's quotes (31 measurements across 9 papers with values). Mismatches: 0.
verification.check_b_reread: Method: after extraction, every primary source was re-read a second time in the same session (PubMed abstract pages re-opened for PMID 2301503, 1635729, 2386134, 3394740, 2222618, 3061844; journal abstract page re-opened for Peters 1993; PMC full texts re-read / find-verified for PMC7613564 and PMC12032418) and each extracted value was compared against the fresh text. Result: 38 of 38 numeric values consistent with the re-read source text. Mismatches: 0 (no value was altered; had any mismatch appeared it would have been flagged here rather than silently corrected). Not applicable: the 4 papers with no extracted values (armitage1980, vince1985, walker1971, nyman1991) had nothing to re-check; their no-number status was itself confirmed on the second look where a source was reachable (armitage1980 abstract confirmed number-free). Excluded by design: the 2 derived values (richards1992 endpoint slope approx. 2.7 dB/octave; benzaquen1990 background fall approx. 8.6 dB/octave) are my arithmetic from extracted endpoints, are stored separately under derived_values, and were not part of either check.
